title: Matplotlib
description: Visualize data effectively using different chart types and improve data storytelling.
objectives: Choose the right chart type for the question being asked.
Build line, bar, scatter, and histogram plots from a DataFrame.
Label every chart so it can be read without explanation.
Use legends, grids, and subplots to make comparisons clear.

slides.title: Matplotlib
slides.lead: A chart is an argument. The type you choose decides which comparison your reader can actually make.
bullets: Line — change over time
Bar — compare categories
Scatter — relationship between two numbers
Histogram — distribution of one number
Import convention: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

slides.title: Line chart — change over time
slides.lead: Use a line only when the x axis has a natural order, usually time. Never for unordered categories.

slides.title: Bar chart — compare categories
slides.lead: Bars must start at zero — the length is the comparison. Sort them by value unless the order carries meaning.

body: # value labels beat a y-axis grid for a small number of bars

slides.note: Use barh when the category names are long — horizontal labels stay readable without rotating them.

slides.title: Scatter plot — relationship between two numbers
slides.lead: Every point is one record. Use it to see correlation, clusters, and outliers.
slides.note: alpha below 1 reveals where points pile up. With thousands of records, overlapping dots otherwise hide the density.

slides.title: Histogram — distribution of one number
slides.lead: A histogram bins one numeric column and counts how many records fall into each bin.
slides.note: Bin count changes the story. Try 10, 20, and 50 on the same data before you settle — too few hides shape, too many shows noise.

slides.title: A chart nobody has to explain
slides.lead: If someone sees the chart with no caption and no presenter, they should still know what it says.
bullets: Title states the finding, not the columns — "Sales grew 58% in Q1", not "Sales chart"
Both axes labelled, with units in brackets
Tick labels rotated if they overlap: ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45)
Source and date somewhere on the figure
Annotate the one point that matters instead of all of them

body: ax.set_title("Scores rose after the tutoring programme", fontsize=14, pad=12)

slides.title: Legends — only when you need one
slides.lead: A legend is needed when one chart shows more than one series. With a single series it is noise.

slides.note: Labelling the end of each line directly is usually better than a legend — the reader stops having to match colours.

slides.title: Grid, styling, and subplots
slides.lead: A faint grid helps readers estimate values. Anything heavier competes with the data.

body: ax.set_axisbelow(True)          # grid behind the bars, not on top

slides.title: Practice: four charts, one dataset
slides.lead: Using your cleaned dataset from Module 04, produce one of each chart type — fully labelled.
bullets: A line chart of a value over time
A sorted horizontal bar chart of a categorical count
A scatter plot of two numeric columns, with the correlation printed
A histogram with a mean line
Combine the best two into one figure with plt.subplots(1, 2)
slides.note: Write the title of each chart as the finding it shows. If you cannot state a finding, the chart is not worth keeping.

slides.title: Module 05 recap
slides.lead: You can now take a question from data to a chart someone else can read.
bullets: fig, ax = plt.subplots() is the pattern to learn
Chart type follows the question: trend, comparison, relationship, distribution
Titles state findings; axes always carry labels and units
Legends only for multiple series; grids stay faint and behind
savefig with bbox_inches="tight" for anything you present
